epigraph.text: Duhamel's Principle always suffices and requires no guessing.
epigraph.by: §3.4, on why this book skips the guess-a-particular-solution ritual

cards.q: Linear systems escape the local-only limit of Picard–Lindelöf. State the theorem and say what powers the proof.
cards.a:
Theorem 3.1.1. If A(t) is continuous on all of ℝ, then every solution of ẋ = A(t)x has maximal interval of existence equal to all of (−∞, ∞).

The proof is Gronwall plus finite-time blowup. Suppose the interval stopped at β < ∞. Blowup (Thm 2.3.8) forces ‖x(t)‖ → ∞ as t → β. But from the integral form,

‖x(t)‖ ≤ ‖x₀‖ + ∫t₀t L‖x(s)‖ ds  ⇒   ‖x(t)‖ ≤ ‖x₀‖eL(t−t₀)
with L = sup‖A‖ finite by continuity on the compact [t₀,β]. The bound stays finite at β, contradicting blowup.

r.rot: chapter 2 kept apologizing that solutions might die young. linear systems don't. ever. the reason: to stop existing in finite time you have to run off to infinity, but gronwall says a linear system can only grow exponentially — and exponential is still finite at any finite time. so it can't get to infinity in time to quit. it lives forever, no exceptions.
r.ex: Contrast ẋ = x² from §2.1, which detonates at t₀ + 1/x₀. That system is nonlinear, so its growth isn't bounded by any e<sup>Lt</sup>, and it outruns every exponential.
r.why: This is the payoff for the analysis in Ch 2 and it's why linear systems are the case you can actually build theory on. Global existence means phase portraits, stability, and long-run behaviour are all well defined — none of which you can assume for a general nonlinear system.
r.math: Continuity on compact [t₀,β] ⇒ L = sup‖A(t)‖ < ∞. Gronwall with u = ‖x‖, φ ≡ L. Bounded at β contradicts Thm 2.3.8.

cards.q: Why does the whole chapter open with the homogeneous case when the system of interest is ẋ = A(t)x + b(t)?
cards.a:
Because the inhomogeneous solution set is a coset of the homogeneous one. If x₁ and x₂ both solve the full system (3.1), their difference solves the homogeneous system (3.2):
(x₁ − x₂)̇ = A(t)x₁ + b(t) − A(t)x₂ − b(t) = A(t)(x₁ − x₂)
So one particular solution + every homogeneous solution = every solution. That splits the work in two: §3.1–§3.3 build the homogeneous theory, and §3.4 supplies the one particular solution via Duhamel.

The chapter also justifies spending this long on linear systems at all: linearization is the main tool for nonlinear ODEs, so the linear theory is a prerequisite even for people who only care about nonlinear problems.

r.rot: same trick as Ax = b in linear algebra. the general solution is one answer you found somehow, plus the entire null space. so you never have to solve the hard forced problem more than once — find a single particular solution and the homogeneous theory fills in the rest for free. that's why b(t) gets benched until §3.4.
r.ex: Concretely: the damped oscillator with no forcing is homogeneous. Push it with an external force b(t) and every possible response is that forced response plus whatever the unforced spring was already doing.
r.why: It tells you what kind of object a solution set is — an affine subspace, not a vector space — and it means the fundamental matrix Φ(t) built in the homogeneous case does double duty in the inhomogeneous case. Without this, §3.4 would need its own theory from scratch.
r.math: Solutions of (3.1) = x<sub>p</sub> + ker, where ker is the n-dimensional solution space of (3.2). Affine, dimension n.

cards.q: Theorem 3.1.1 leans on Existence and Uniqueness. Where exactly does f(x,t) = A(t)x + b(t) earn locally Lipschitz?
cards.a:
Directly from the operator norm, with continuity doing the work:
‖f(x₁,t) − f(x₂,t)‖ = ‖A(t)(x₁ − x₂)‖ ≤ ‖A(t)‖⋅‖x₁ − x₂‖ ≤ L‖x₁ − x₂‖
with L = supt∈I‖A(t)‖, finite because A is continuous and I is compact. Note what drops out: b(t) cancels, so forcing never affects the Lipschitz constant.

Two things are worth noticing. First, the constant is uniform in x — a linear map has the same Lipschitz constant everywhere, which is exactly why the local theorem upgrades to a global one. Second, b(t) only needs to be continuous, not Lipschitz, because it is not a function of x.

r.rot: locally lipschitz usually means 'don't go too far from where you started or the bound dies'. for a linear system the bound never dies — ‖A‖ is the slope and it's the same slope at every x. you get the local theorem's conclusion with a constant that works globally, which is the entire reason linear systems never blow up.
r.ex: Compare f(x) = x². Its Lipschitz constant on |x| ≤ R is 2R, which grows without bound as you move out. That unboundedness is exactly the room ẋ = x² needs to reach infinity in finite time.
r.why: This is the hinge of the whole chapter. Everything downstream — global existence, the fundamental matrix being defined for all t, phase portraits — requires E&U to apply at every point with no caveats, and this computation is what buys that.
r.math: L = sup<sub>t∈I</sub>‖A(t)‖ < ∞ on compact I. Lipschitz in x, uniformly; b(t) cancels out of the difference.

cards.q: Define the fundamental matrix and the principal fundamental matrix. What does Φ(t) let you do in one step?
cards.a:
Solutions of ẋ = A(t)x form a vector space, and v ↦ x(t) with x(t₀) = v is a linear map. So a basis of initial conditions gives a basis of solutions.

Definition 3.1.3. For a basis {v₁,…,vn} of ℝn, let xk solve the system with xk(t₀) = vk. The matrix of columns Φ(t) = [x₁(t) ··· xn(t)] is the fundamental matrix. If vk = ek so that Φ(t₀) = I, it's the principal fundamental matrix.

Φ̇(t) = A(t)Φ(t),   and  x(t) = Φ(t)v solves the IVP with x(t₀) = v
One matrix-vector product gives the solution for any initial condition.

r.rot: solve the system n times, once for each basis direction, and stack the answers as columns. that matrix is now a machine: hand it any starting vector and it hands back the whole trajectory. you did the work n times and bought yourself infinitely many solutions. principal just means you used the standard basis so Φ(t₀) = I, which makes the bookkeeping free.
r.ex: Prop 3.1.4: the columns are linearly independent for all t. If they weren't, two different initial conditions would produce the same solution, contradicting uniqueness from Ch 2.
r.why: This is the structural payoff of linearity, and it's the object every later result is stated about — AJL computes its determinant, Duhamel uses its inverse. Nonlinear systems have no analogue: you cannot combine two solutions to get a third.
r.math: Φ̇ = AΦ, Φ(t₀) = [v₁ ··· v<sub>n</sub>]. Principal: Φ(t₀) = I. Solution set is an n-dimensional vector space.

cards.q: Define the matrix exponential and list the properties of Theorem 3.1.8. Which one has a hypothesis you must not forget?
cards.a:
etA = Σk≥0 (tA)k/k!
Theorem 3.1.8. (i) e0 = I. (ii) etAesA = e(t+s)A. (iii) (etA)−1 = e−tA, so etA is always invertible. (iv) d/dt etA = AetA = etAA. (vi) A = PDP−1 ⇒ etA = PetDP−1.

(v) is the one with the trap: et(A+B) = etAetB only if AB = BA. Matrices generally don't commute, so this generally fails.

Cor 3.1.9: for the autonomous system ẋ = Ax, the principal fundamental matrix is Φ(t) = e(t−t₀)A.

r.rot: same taylor series as the scalar exponential, just feed it a matrix. almost every rule survives — except the one everybody wants. e<sup>A+B</sup> ≠ e<sup>A</sup>e<sup>B</sup> unless A and B commute, and matrices mostly don't. that single failure is why matrix exponentials are hard and why half of numerical linear algebra exists.
r.ex: Remark 3.1.7: Cayley–Hamilton says p(A) = 0 for the characteristic polynomial, so A<sup>n</sup> and every higher power collapse to polynomials of degree ≤ n−1. The infinite series is secretly a polynomial of degree at most n−1.
r.why: etA is the solution operator for every constant-coefficient linear system, so this one object solves the whole class. The invertibility in (iii) is what makes Duhamel's Φ(s)−1 legal in §3.4.
r.math: Don't compute via the series: each product costs ~O(n³) and p iterations gives O(pn³). §3.2 gives the spectral route instead.

cards.q: A is not diagonalizable. What are your options for etA, and what does the nilpotent case buy you?
cards.a:
Nilpotent A. If Ak = 0 the series (3.6) terminates — etA is a polynomial you can write down exactly.
A = [[−1,1],[−1,1]], A² = 0  ⇒  etA = I + tA = [[1−t, t],[−t, 1+t]]
Splitting off a commuting piece. Write A = λI + N. Since λI commutes with everything, Theorem 3.1.8(v) applies, so etA = eλtetN, and etN is the terminating series above.
A = [[1,2],[0,1]] = I + B, B² = 0  ⇒  etA = et(I + tB) = et[[1,2t],[0,1]]
That tet term is the fingerprint of a defective eigenvalue: polynomial growth multiplying the exponential.

r.rot: diagonalization failed, so you cheat differently. nilpotent matrices kill themselves after a few powers, so the infinite series is actually finite — just add up three terms and stop. and any jordan-ish matrix splits as (scalar)⋅I + nilpotent, where the scalar part commutes with everything so the forbidden product rule becomes legal. the t sitting next to e<sup>t</sup> in the answer is the defect showing up in the solution.
r.ex: This is where repeated roots in a second-order ODE come from. y″ − 2y′ + y = 0 has solutions e<sup>t</sup> and te<sup>t</sup> — that second one is precisely the e<sup>λt</sup>(I + tN) above, viewed as a system.
r.why: Remark 3.1.15 warns that defective matrices are not a pathology to route around: they are exactly where bifurcations happen as a model's parameters change, which is often the phenomenon you built the model to see. So you need a method that works there.
r.math: A = λI + N, N<sup>k</sup> = 0, [λI, N] = 0 ⇒ e<sup>tA</sup> = e<sup>λt</sup>Σ<sub>j<k</sub> t<sup>j</sup>N<sup>j</sup>/j!. Cayley–Hamilton already bounds the degree at n−1.

cards.q: Diagonalization gives e<sup>tA</sup> = Pe<sup>tΛ</sup>P<sup>−1</sup>. When is that numerically a bad idea, and what replaces it?
cards.a:
The formula is fine; P−1 is the problem. If P is ill conditioned — its largest-to-smallest singular value ratio is huge, which happens when two eigenvectors are nearly parallel — then inverting it amplifies error, and tiny perturbations in A produce huge errors in etA.

Best case: A normal. Then A is orthonormally diagonalizable, P is as well conditioned as a matrix can be, and P−1 = PH — no inversion at all.

The general fix: Schur. Schur's Lemma writes A = UTUH with T upper triangular and U orthonormal. Theorem 3.1.8(vi) then gives etA = UetTUH, and UH = U−1 is free and perfectly conditioned. Separate algorithms handle etT for triangular T.

r.rot: P<sup>−1</sup> is where the numerical pain lives. if two eigenvectors point almost the same direction, P is nearly singular, inverting it is a disaster, and your beautiful exact formula returns garbage. schur's move: give up on diagonal, settle for triangular, but insist the change of basis be orthonormal — then the inverse is the conjugate transpose, which costs nothing and loses nothing.
r.ex: Nearly parallel eigenvectors happen precisely when eigenvalues are nearly repeated — a matrix close to a defective one. So the analytically awkward case and the numerically awkward case are the same case.
r.why: It separates 'the formula is true' from 'the formula is computable'. Theorem 3.1.8(vi) holds for any similarity, so you get to choose the similarity, and the right criterion is conditioning, not diagonality.
r.math: κ(P) = σ<sub>max</sub>/σ<sub>min</sub>. Normal A ⇒ κ(P) = 1. Schur: A = UTU<sup>H</sup>, κ(U) = 1, e<sup>tA</sup> = Ue<sup>tT</sup>U<sup>H</sup>.

cards.q: A is real but its eigenvalues are a + ib and a − ib. How do you get a real-valued e<sup>tA</sup> out of that?
cards.a:
Refuse to leave ℝ. Complex eigenvalues of a real matrix come in conjugate pairs, and the eigenvectors can be chosen as u ± iv with u, v real. Put those real parts side by side as Q = [u v] ∈ M₂(ℝ); then
Q−1AQ = C = [[a, b],[−b, a]]
a real 2×2 block, no complex numbers anywhere. Now split it:
C = [[a,0],[0,a]] + [[0,b],[−b,0]]
The first summand is a multiple of I, so it commutes with the second and Theorem 3.1.8(v) is legal:
etC = eat⋅[[cos bt, sin bt],[−sin bt, cos bt]]
a is the growth rate, b is the rotation rate. Spirals.

r.rot: complex eigenvalues don't mean complex answers — they mean rotation. take the real and imaginary parts of the eigenvector as your two basis vectors, and in that basis A is just 'scale by a, spin at rate b'. exponentiate: eat times a rotation matrix. the trajectory spirals out if a > 0, in if a < 0, and rides a closed circle if a = 0.
r.ex: The underdamped oscillator. Complex pair with a < 0 gives e<sup>at</sup>cos(bt) — oscillation inside a decaying envelope, which is exactly what a real spring with friction does.
r.why: It keeps the whole real-variable theory closed: you never have to interpret a complex trajectory physically. It also gives the visual vocabulary for phase portraits — sign of the real part decides in/out, the imaginary part decides how fast it spins.
r.math: λ = a ± ib, eigenvectors u ± iv, Q = [u v]. Q<sup>−1</sup>AQ = C; e<sup>tC</sup> = e<sup>at</sup>R(bt), R a rotation. The span of {u,v} is A-invariant.

cards.q: Define the resolvent of A. What does Cramer's Rule tell you about its entries, and where are its poles?
cards.a:
RA(z) = (zI − A)−1
Cramer's Rule makes its structure explicit:
RA(z) = adj(zI − A) / det(zI − A)
Every entry is a rational function — a polynomial from the adjugate over the characteristic polynomial. So R(z) is defined and holomorphic on all of ℂ except at the eigenvalues, where the denominator vanishes.

That is the point: the poles of the resolvent are exactly σ(A), and the order of the pole at λ is bounded by its algebraic multiplicity. All of the spectral information about A is encoded as the singularity structure of one matrix-valued rational function, which is what lets contour integration extract it.

r.rot: take zI − A and invert it. by cramer that's (polynomial stuff) / (characteristic polynomial), so each entry is a ratio of polynomials. it blows up exactly at the eigenvalues and nowhere else. that's the whole trick: you've turned 'the eigenvalues of A' into 'the poles of this function', and complex analysis has an entire toolkit for poles.
r.ex: For A = [[1,2],[0,1]]: det(zI − A) = (z−1)², so R(z) = [[1/(z−1), 2/(z−1)²],[0, 1/(z−1)]]. One eigenvalue, and the double pole in the corner is the defect showing itself.
r.why: It converts linear algebra into complex analysis. Once eigenvalues are poles, residues give you projections and Cauchy's formula gives you f(A) — and none of it requires A to be diagonalizable, which is where ordinary eigenvector methods quit.
r.math: R(z) = adj(zI−A)/p(z), p the characteristic polynomial. Poles = σ(A); pole order at λ is m<sub>λ</sub> ≤ n<sub>λ</sub> (the algebraic multiplicity).

cards.q: State the Spectral Resolution Formula. How does it define f(A) for a matrix?
cards.a:
Theorem 3.2.2. If f has a power series at 0 with radius of convergence b > r(A), then for any positively-oriented simple closed contour Γ containing σ(A),
f(A) = (1/2πi) ∮Γ f(z)R(z) dz
This is Cauchy's integral formula with a matrix in the place of a number. The matrix exponential is the case f(z) = etz:
etA = (1/2πi) ∮Γ etzR(z) dz   (3.13)

Two features earn their keep. The contour doesn't matter — any curve enclosing the spectrum gives the same answer, because the integrand is holomorphic off σ(A). And no diagonalization is required: the formula never mentions eigenvectors, so it works for defective A where P−1ΛP does not exist.

r.rot: you already know how to apply a function to a number. this says: to apply f to a matrix, integrate f(z) against the resolvent around a loop that fences in all the eigenvalues. by the residue theorem the answer only depends on what happens at the poles — i.e. at the eigenvalues — so the loop's exact shape is irrelevant. set f = etz and you have the matrix exponential with no eigenvectors in sight.
r.ex: Example 3.2.3 runs it on A = [[1,2],[0,1]]: e<sup>tz</sup>R(z) has a double pole at z = 1, residues e<sup>t</sup> and 2te<sup>t</sup>, giving e<sup>tA</sup> = [[e<sup>t</sup>, 2te<sup>t</sup>],[0, e<sup>t</sup>]] — the same answer the nilpotent split gave in Example 3.1.14.
r.why: It is the definition that generalizes. Series definitions need convergence, diagonalization needs eigenvectors; the contour integral needs only holomorphy near the spectrum, and it extends verbatim to bounded operators on a Banach space.
r.math: Requires f holomorphic on an open set containing σ(A). Γ positively oriented, simple, closed, encircling σ(A). Also known as Riesz functional calculus.

cards.q: Define the eigenprojection and eigennilpotent, and state the spectral decomposition of A.
cards.a:
Definition 3.2.4. For a contour Γ encircling only λ ∈ σ(A), with resolvent R(z) = (zI − A)−1:
Pλ = 12πi∮Γ R(z)dz    Dλ = 12πi∮Γ(z − λ)R(z)dz
Pλ is the eigenprojection, Dλ the eigennilpotent, with order mλ the least m with Dλm = 0.

Thm 3.2.6: A = Σλ(λPλ + Dλ).

Prop 3.2.5: ΣPλ = I; Pλ² = Pλ; APλ = PλA; PλPλ′ = 0 for λ ≠ λ′; Dλ = (A − λI)Pλ; and Dλnλ = 0 for algebraic multiplicity nλ.

r.rot: chop A into one piece per eigenvalue. each piece is λ times a projection (the diagonalizable part) plus a nilpotent (the part that refuses to diagonalize, and dies after finitely many powers). the projections add to I and annihilate each other, so they carve ℝ<sup>n</sup> into independent chunks. it's the jordan form again — but built by contour integration instead of by finding a basis, which matters because contour integrals are numerically stable and jordan bases are not.
r.ex: If A is semisimple (diagonalizable), every D<sub>λ</sub> = 0 and the decomposition is just A = ΣλP<sub>λ</sub>. Remark 3.1.15 notes most matrices are semisimple, so the nilpotent parts are the exceptional case.
r.why: The book is explicit that the Jordan decomposition is not well conditioned, so in floating point it isn't really computable. Eigenprojections are the computable substitute, and they're what makes the next result work.
r.math: R<sub>A</sub>(z) = Σ<sub>λ</sub>[P<sub>λ</sub>/(z−λ) + Σ<sub>k=1</sub><sup>m<sub>λ</sub>−1</sup> D<sub>λ</sub><sup>k</sup>/(z−λ)<sup>k+1</sup>]. Each resolvent entry is rational by Cramer's rule.

cards.q: Proposition 3.2.5 lists seven properties of P<sub>λ</sub> and D<sub>λ</sub>. Which two let you skip the contour integrals entirely?
cards.a:
(i) Σλ∈σ(A) Pλ = I and (v) Dλ = (A − λI)Pλ.

Together they mean you compute one eigenprojection by residue and get everything else by algebra. With two eigenvalues: find P₃ from the residue, then P₂ = I − P₃, then D₂ = (A − 2I)P₂. No second integral.

The rest describe the structure: (ii) Pλ² = Pλ, they are projections. (iii) APλ = PλA. (iv) PλPλ′ = PλDλ′ = 0 for λ ≠ λ′ — different eigenvalues live in independent pieces. (vi) PλDλ = Dλ. (vii) Dλnλ = 0, so mλ ≤ nλ: the nilpotent dies by the algebraic multiplicity.

r.rot: (i) and (v) are the laziness properties. the P's add up to the identity, so the last one is just I minus the others — you never compute all of them. and D isn't a separate mystery object, it's literally (A − λI) hitting P. so one honest residue calculation plus two subtractions gets you the entire spectral decomposition.
r.ex: Example 3.2.10, A = [[1,2],[0,1]]: only one eigenvalue, so (i) forces P₁ = I outright, and (v) gives D₁ = A − I = [[0,2],[0,0]]. Zero integrals computed, and e<sup>tA</sup> = e<sup>t</sup>(I + tD₁).
r.why: It turns a theoretical construction into something you can do by hand on an exam. (vii) is separately load-bearing: it caps the sum in Corollary 3.2.9 at n<sub>λ</sub> terms, so the formula for e<sup>tA</sup> is always a finite sum.
r.math: The P<sub>λ</sub> are a complete set of mutually orthogonal idempotents commuting with A. Range P<sub>λ</sub> = the generalized eigenspace, dim = n<sub>λ</sub>.

cards.q: State the Spectral Mapping Theorem. What does it predict about the eigenvalues of e<sup>tA</sup>?
cards.a:
Theorem 3.2.7. If f is holomorphic on an open disk containing σ(A), then
σ(f(A)) = f(σ(A))
and moreover, an eigenvector x of A for λ is an eigenvector of f(A) for f(λ) — the eigenvectors don't move.

For f(z) = etz: the eigenvalues of etA are exactly etλ for λ ∈ σ(A). Read as dynamics, with λ = a + ib:

|etλ| = eat
so the real parts of the eigenvalues of A alone decide growth or decay, and the imaginary parts contribute rotation of modulus 1. Note also that etλ is never 0, which re-proves that etA is invertible.

r.rot: apply a function to a matrix, and the eigenvalues get the same function applied to them. nothing more complicated than that. so the eigenvalues of e<sup>tA</sup> are just e<sup>tλ</sup>. take absolute values and the imaginary part vanishes — only Re(λ) survives. that one line is why every stability criterion you will ever see is about the real parts of eigenvalues.
r.ex: A with σ(A) = {−1, −1000} (the stiff oscillator of Example 3.1.11): e<sup>tA</sup> has eigenvalues e<sup>−t</sup> and e<sup>−1000t</sup>. Both decay, but at wildly different rates — and that ratio is precisely the stiffness that wrecks explicit numerical methods in Ch 4.
r.why: It is the bridge from a static algebraic quantity to long-run behaviour. Everything in stability theory — Reλ < 0 means the origin attracts, Reλ > 0 means it repels — is this theorem applied to f(z) = e<sup>tz</sup>.
r.math: σ(e<sup>tA</sup>) = e<sup>tσ(A)</sup>. |e<sup>t(a+ib)</sup>| = e<sup>at</sup>. 0 ∉ σ(e<sup>tA</sup>) ⇒ e<sup>tA</sup> invertible, matching Thm 3.1.8(iii).

cards.q: Give the spectral formula for e<sup>tA</sup>. Why is it better than summing the series?
cards.a:
Corollary 3.2.9.
etA = Σλ∈σ(A) etλ[ Pλ + Σk=1mλ−1 tkDλkk! ]
It follows from Thm 3.2.8 (mapping the spectral decomposition), which computes any holomorphic f(A) by applying f to each eigenvalue and its Taylor coefficients to the nilpotents.

Why it's better: the sum is finite — one term per eigenvalue, and the inner sum stops at mλ−1 because Dλ is nilpotent. No convergence, no truncation error, and you can read the dynamics straight off: each mode grows like etλ, with polynomial-in-t corrections exactly where A fails to diagonalize.

r.rot: the infinite series becomes a finite sum. one term per eigenvalue, and the nilpotent bits terminate on their own because Dm = 0. and the best part is you can read it: the etλ factors say how fast each mode grows or decays, and the tk terms only appear where the matrix wouldn't diagonalize. every stability fact you'll ever want about ẋ = Ax is sitting in this formula.
r.ex: Diagonalizable A: all D<sub>λ</sub> = 0 and it collapses to e<sup>tA</sup> = Σe<sup>tλ</sup>P<sub>λ</sub>. A defective eigenvalue contributes te<sup>tλ</sup>, t²e<sup>tλ</sup>/2, and so on — the resonance terms you meet in a critically damped oscillator.
r.why: This is the concrete method for solving any constant-coefficient linear system, and it's the bridge to stability theory: Re(λ) < 0 for all eigenvalues means every term decays and the origin attracts. The Spectral Mapping Theorem (3.2.7), σ(f(A)) = f(σ(A)), is the general statement behind it.
r.math: Requires f holomorphic on an open set containing σ(A). exp is entire, so it always applies.

cards.q: Remark 3.2.13 says not to compute this way. If spectral calculus is impractical, what is it for?
cards.a:
It is a proof tool, not an algorithm. Computing R(z) = (zI − A)−1 symbolically means an n×n adjugate — n² determinants of polynomial matrices — and the cost is prohibitive as n grows. Chapter 4's numerical methods are what you actually run.

What it gives you instead is the exact form of every solution. Corollary 3.2.9 says

etA = Σλ etλ[Pλ + Σk<mλ (tk/k!)Dλk]
so every solution of ẋ = Ax is a sum of terms tkeλt with k < mλ, for eigenvalues λ of A. That single structural fact — exponentials, possibly multiplied by polynomials of degree less than the eigennilpotent order — is what you carry into every stability argument, and no amount of floating-point output would establish it.

There is a second, harder warning: the Jordan decomposition is always possible in exact arithmetic but is not a well-conditioned problem, so in floating point it is not really computable.

r.rot: nobody actually computes a resolvent for a 50×50 matrix. the payoff isn't the number, it's the shape of the answer: every solution is exponentials times polynomials, full stop. polynomials only show up when an eigenvalue is defective, and they can't outrank its multiplicity. knowing that lets you argue about t → ∞ without ever computing anything — e−t beats any power of t, so decay wins.
r.ex: Example 3.2.12 shows the price: a 4×4 with one defective eigenvalue takes a page of adjugate work, three eigenprojection entries, and D₁² — and the answer still has only e<sup>t</sup>, te<sup>t</sup>, t²e<sup>t</sup>/2 and e<sup>7t</sup> in it.
r.why: It marks the line between theory and computation that Chapter 4 formalizes. And it explains the earlier numerical advice: since Jordan form is uncomputable in floating point, the practical routes are the well-conditioned ones — Schur, or a direct approximation of the exponential.
r.math: Terms are t<sup>k</sup>e<sup>λt</sup>, 0 ≤ k < m<sub>λ</sub> ≤ n<sub>λ</sub>. Growth is governed by Reλ, since t<sup>k</sup>e<sup>at</sup> → 0 for any k when a < 0.

cards.q: For scalars, ẋ = a(t)x solves as exp(∫a). Why does the matrix version usually fail, and when does it work?
cards.a:
The natural guess Φ(t) = exp(∫t₀tA(s)ds) is usually wrong. Differentiating it needs d/dt eB(t) = Ḃ(t)eB(t), which requires B(t) and Ḃ(t) to commute — the same non-commutativity trap as Theorem 3.1.8(v).

Prop 3.3.1. If A is continuous and A(s)A(t) = A(t)A(s) for all s,t, then the guess is the principal fundamental matrix solution.

Proof sketch: with B(t) = ∫A, commutativity gives B(t)A(t) = ∫A(s)A(t)ds = A(t)∫A(s)ds = A(t)B(t), which is exactly what licenses the differentiation.

Unexample 3.3.2 shows a non-commuting A where it fails.

r.rot: you want to do the obvious thing: integrate A and exponentiate, like the scalar case. it doesn't work. the reason is the same one that broke eA+B — A at one time doesn't commute with A at another time, so the derivative rule you need isn't true. if A(s) and A(t) do commute for every pair, the trick is legal. that's a strong hypothesis and most A(t) fail it.
r.ex: A(t) commutes with itself across time when, say, A(t) = f(t)M for a fixed matrix M — then everything is a scalar multiple of M and scalars commute. Mix two non-commuting matrices with t-dependent weights and it breaks.
r.why: This is why nonautonomous linear systems are genuinely harder than autonomous ones and generally have no closed-form fundamental matrix. Everything after this section is about what you can still compute without one — namely the determinant.
r.math: Needs d/dt e<sup>B(t)</sup> = Ḃe<sup>B</sup>, valid when [B(t), Ḃ(t)] = 0.

cards.q: Trace the failure all the way down: why can't you differentiate exp(∫A(s)ds) the usual way?
cards.a:
Because the power rule is false for matrix-valued functions. The product rule still holds, but it will not collapse:
d/dt B² = d/dt (B⋅B) = ḂB + BḂ
and that equals 2ḂB only if B commutes with Ḃ. Since eB is built from all the powers Bk, every term of the termwise derivative inherits the problem.

Proposition 3.3.1's proof is exactly the repair. Assume A(s)A(t) = A(t)A(s) for all s,t, and with B(t) = ∫t₀tA(s)ds you can pull A(t) through the integral:

B(t)A(t) = ∫A(s)A(t)ds = A(t)∫A(s)ds = A(t)B(t)  (3.22)
Induction then gives d/dt Bk = kABk−1, the power rule is restored term by term, and summing the (uniformly convergent) series gives Φ̇ = AΦ.

r.rot: scalars commute, so d/dt(b²) = 2ḃb and nobody thinks twice. matrices don't, so you get ḂB + BḂ and those two terms are different objects you cannot add into one. the exponential is an infinite pile of powers, so the bug propagates everywhere. assume A(s) and A(t) commute for every pair of times and the bug disappears — but that's a strong assumption almost nothing satisfies.
r.ex: Where the induction actually bites: d/dt B<sup>k</sup> = (d/dt B<sup>k−1</sup>)B + B<sup>k−1</sup>Ḃ = (k−1)AB<sup>k−2</sup>B + B<sup>k−1</sup>A. The last term is only AB<sup>k−1</sup> because (3.22) lets A move left past every copy of B.
r.why: Non-commutativity is the single obstruction that separates the autonomous case (where e<sup>(t−t₀)A</sup> settles everything) from the nonautonomous one. Naming it precisely tells you what to check before using any formula imported from scalar ODEs.
r.math: Need [B(t), Ḃ(t)] = 0. Hypothesis [A(s), A(t)] = 0 ∀s,t ⇒ [B(t), A(t)] = 0. Termwise differentiation is legal because the series converges uniformly on compacts.

cards.q: State the Abel–Jacobi–Liouville formula and two corollaries.
cards.a:
Theorem 3.3.3 (AJL). If Φ̇(t) = A(t)Φ(t), then
det Φ(t) = det Φ(t₀) · exp( ∫t₀t tr A(s) ds )
The determinant of a fundamental matrix is called the Wronskian. Even when you cannot compute Φ, you can always compute its determinant — from the trace alone.

Cor 3.3.8: Φ(t) is nonsingular for all t, since the exponential never vanishes and detΦ(t₀) ≠ 0.

Cor 3.3.9 (Jacobi's formula): for constant A, det(etA) = et·tr A.

r.rot: you usually can't write down Φ(t). but its determinant you can always get, and it only depends on the trace — the cheapest number attached to A. that's a strange and useful bargain. and since exp is never zero, Φ can never go singular, which re-proves that your n solutions stay independent forever.
r.ex: Jacobi's formula det(e<sup>tA</sup>) = e<sup>t·tr A</sup> is the matrix version of ‘determinant is the product of eigenvalues, trace is their sum’, exponentiated. tr A = 0 means volume is preserved — that's what makes a system Hamiltonian.
r.why: The nonsingularity corollary is what Duhamel's proof leans on in §3.4 when it needs Φ(s)<sup>−1</sup>. Geometrically, detΦ is how the flow scales volume in phase space, and AJL says the trace is the instantaneous rate.
r.math: d/dt detΦ = (tr A)detΦ. Never zero, so independence of the columns persists for all t.

cards.q: Unexample 3.3.2 — how do you show a given A(t) fails the commuting hypothesis?
cards.a:
You only need two times. Exhibit s and t with A(s)A(t) ≠ A(t)A(s) and the hypothesis is dead. For the nonautonomous matrix of Example 3.1.6, take t = 0 and t = π/2:
A(0) = [[½, 1],[−1, −1]],   A(π/2) = [[−1, 1],[−1, ½]]
A(0)A(π/2) = [[−3/2, 1],[2, −3/2]] ≠ [[−3/2, −2],[−1, −3/2]] = A(π/2)A(0)
Two products, one comparison, done — disproving a universally quantified hypothesis takes a single counterexample, and you never have to touch the general t.

What makes it a genuine unexample rather than a broken system: this A(t) still has a perfectly good fundamental matrix, written out in Example 3.1.6. The system is fine. Only the shortcut exp(∫A) is unavailable.

r.rot: the hypothesis says 'for all s and t'. so to kill it, pick two convenient times — 0 and π/2, because sin and cos are 0 and 1 there — multiply the two matrices in both orders, and point at the difference. the system still has solutions. you just can't get them from the pretty formula.
r.ex: This same A(t) reappears in Example 3.3.7, where AJL correctly predicts detΦ(t) = e<sup>−t/2</sup> from tr A(s) = −½. So the trace result survives non-commutativity even though the exponential formula doesn't.
r.why: It stops you from treating Prop 3.3.1 as the general theory. Commuting families are a thin special case — essentially A(t) = f(t)A₀ and block-diagonal-in-a-fixed-basis situations — and a random time-dependent A almost never qualifies.
r.math: Choose s,t where the entries simplify. Here cos², sin², sin⋅cos take values in {0, 1} at t = 0, π/2.

cards.q: AJL is usually stated as an integral. Give its differential form and say what the trace means geometrically.
cards.a:
The proof of Theorem 3.3.3 actually establishes a differential equation for the Wronskian, and the stated formula is what you get by separating it:
d/dt detΦ(t) = tr(A(t)) ⋅ detΦ(t)
detΦ obeys a scalar linear ODE with coefficient tr A(t).

Geometrically, Φ(t) carries the unit cube spanned by the initial conditions to a parallelepiped at time t, and detΦ(t) is its signed volume. So the equation says:

(relative rate of volume change) = tr A(t)
tr A > 0 expands phase-space volume, tr A < 0 contracts it, tr A = 0 preserves it. The proof is Jacobi's formula: differentiate the determinant one row at a time, recognize each term as det((I − Ejj)Φ + EjjΦ̇), substitute Φ̇ = AΦ, and each factors to ajjdetΦ — summing the diagonal gives the trace.

r.rot: determinant = volume. so tracking detΦ means tracking what the flow does to volumes, and the answer is embarrassingly simple: the volume grows at rate tr A. not the eigenvalues, not the determinant of A — the trace. positive trace, phase space inflates; negative, it collapses; zero, volume is conserved forever and the flow is incompressible.
r.ex: Example 3.3.5: A = [[−1,1],[−1,1]] has trace 0, and sure enough detΦ(t) = 1 for all t. Example 3.3.4: A = [[1,4],[1,1]] has trace 2, and detΦ(t) = e<sup>2t</sup>.
r.why: It gives you one exactly computable quantity in a setting where Φ itself is usually out of reach — and computing tr A(t) is free. It is also the linear ancestor of Liouville's theorem in Hamiltonian mechanics, where tr A = 0 is why phase-space volume is conserved.
r.math: d/dt detΦ = tr(A)detΦ, separable. Constant A: det(e<sup>tA</sup>) = e<sup>t⋅tr A</sup>, Cor 3.3.9.

cards.q: You already know one solution of a 2×2 nonautonomous system. How does AJL hand you the second?
cards.a:
Reduction of order. The known solution is one column of some fundamental matrix; call the unknown column z(t) and let AJL constrain the determinant.

Example 3.3.6. Given x = (1, t) solving ẋ = [[1, −1/t],[1+t, −1]]x on (0,∞), write Φ = [[z₁, 1],[z₂, t]]. Here tr A(s) = 0, so AJL says detΦ is constant:

c = t z₁(t) − z₂(t)  (3.25)
Now feed that back into the ODE for z. The first component gives ż₁ = z₁ − z₂/t = (tz₁ − z₂)/t = c/t — a first-order scalar equation, because (3.25) collapsed the coupling. Integrate: z₁ = c log t + d, and (3.25) returns z₂ = ct log t + dt − c.

Two unknown functions became one, and the system became a quadrature.

r.rot: classic trick, new justification. you know one solution; the second is unknown. AJL pins down the determinant of the matrix holding both, which is one algebraic equation linking the two unknown components. use it to eliminate one, and the surviving equation is a single scalar ODE you can just integrate. n unknowns became n−1.
r.ex: Watch the collapse: ż₁ = z₁ − z₂/t looks coupled, but rewriting it as (tz₁ − z₂)/t lets you substitute the constant c straight in. That rewriting is the entire step.
r.why: It is the practical use of AJL. For nonautonomous systems you have no e<sup>tA</sup> and no general method, so 'guess or find one solution, get the rest' is often the only route open — and this is the same reduction-of-order you met for second-order scalar ODEs, now explained.
r.math: Works for any n: AJL gives one relation among the n unknown entries of the new column, cutting the system to n−1. Needs detΦ(t₀) ≠ 0, i.e. the new column independent of the known one.

cards.q: Does global existence survive adding a forcing term b(t)?
cards.a:
Yes. Theorem 3.4.1. If A(t) and b(t) are both continuous on all of ℝ, then the maximal interval of existence for ẋ = A(t)x + b(t) is all of (−∞, ∞).

This is the promise Remark 3.1.2 made back in §3.1 — Theorem 3.1.1 was stated for the homogeneous case, and the inhomogeneous version was deferred to here.

Same machinery: existence and uniqueness gives a local solution, Gronwall bounds its growth by an exponential, and finite-time blowup then can't happen.

r.rot: adding forcing doesn't break anything, as long as the forcing itself is continuous everywhere. still no blowup, still alive for all time. same gronwall argument — the extra b(t) term is bounded on compact intervals so it just rides along inside the bound.
r.ex: A driven oscillator with continuous forcing runs forever. The only way to break it is a forcing term that itself blows up in finite time, which violates the hypothesis.
r.why: Together with Thm 3.1.1 this says linear systems with continuous data are always globally well posed — existence, uniqueness, continuous dependence, on all of ℝ. That is the strongest guarantee in the volume, and nothing nonlinear gets it.
r.math: Same proof as 3.1.1 with ‖ẋ‖ ≤ ‖A‖‖x‖ + ‖b‖; Gronwall still yields an exponential bound.

cards.q: Theorem 3.4.1's proof needs a generalized Gronwall. What changed, and where does b(t) go?
cards.a:
b(t) is not a function of x, so it cannot join the Lipschitz term — it integrates to a constant instead. Continuity of b on the compact [t₀,β] gives
C = ∫t₀β‖b(s)‖ds < ∞
‖x(t)‖ ≤ (‖x₀‖ + C) + ∫t₀t‖A(s)‖⋅‖x(s)‖ds  (3.30)
The generalization: ordinary Gronwall wants a constant out front; this version allows a function α(t), continuous, nonnegative, C¹ with nonnegative derivative. If θ(t) ≤ α(t) + ∫γ(s)θ(s)ds then
θ(t) ≤ α(t)⋅exp(∫atγ(s)ds)
Apply with α = ‖x₀‖ + C, θ = ‖x‖, γ = ‖A‖. The bound is finite at β, contradicting blowup.

r.rot: forcing adds a lump you can't fold into the lipschitz part, because b doesn't depend on x at all. but b is continuous on a closed bounded interval, so its integral is just some finite number C. shove C in with the initial condition, apply gronwall, get an exponential bound again. the forcing changes the constant, not the conclusion.
r.ex: The monotone-α hypothesis is what keeps the proof honest if you need a t-dependent bound — here α happens to be constant, so the plain version would also do, but the general statement is what gets reused later in the book.
r.why: It completes the promise Remark 3.1.2 made in §3.1: global existence is a property of linear systems, not just homogeneous ones. So the whole fundamental-matrix apparatus is safe to use on forced systems for all t.
r.math: Requires A, b continuous on ℝ. α nonneg, C¹, α′ ≥ 0. Conclusion: ‖x(t)‖ ≤ (‖x₀‖+C)exp(∫‖A‖), bounded on bounded t.

cards.q: State Duhamel's Principle and variation of parameters. What's the trick in the proof?
cards.a:
Theorem 3.4.2 (Duhamel). For ẋ = A(t)x + Q(x,t), x(t₀) = x₀, with Φ the principal fundamental matrix of the homogeneous system:
x(t) = Φ(t)x₀ + Φ(t)∫t₀t Φ(s)−1Q(x(s),s) ds
Q need not be linear in x — then it's an implicit equation. Taking Q = b(t) gives Cor 3.4.3, variation of parameters, an explicit solution.

The trick: the ansatz x(t) = Φ(t)h(t) — treat the constant vector in the homogeneous solution as a function. Substituting, the Φ̇h terms cancel on both sides, leaving Φ(t)ḣ(t) = Q, so ḣ = Φ−1Q. Integrate and substitute back.

r.rot: homogeneous solution is Φ(t) times a constant. forcing shows up? let the constant stop being constant. plug Φ(t)h(t) in, and the terms that made Φ a solution cancel themselves out, leaving one clean equation for ḣ. integrate, done. that's the whole method — and note it works even when the forcing is nonlinear, which is why it's a principle and not just a formula.
r.ex: Remark 3.4.4 is pointed: intro ODE courses teach you to guess a particular solution shaped like b(t) — trig forcing, guess trig. The book declines, because Duhamel always works and needs no inspiration.
r.why: It needs Φ(s)<sup>−1</sup> to exist for every s, which is exactly Corollary 3.3.8 from AJL. That's the chapter's structure paying off: nonsingularity was proved two sections earlier precisely so this integral is defined.
r.math: Ansatz x = Φh ⇒ Φ̇h + Φḣ = AΦh + Q. Since AΦ = Φ̇, cancel to Φḣ = Q. h(t₀) = x₀ since Φ(t₀) = I.

cards.q: Remark 3.4.4 declines the standard undetermined-coefficients method. What is the objection, and what is given up?
cards.a:
The objection is stated flatly: Duhamel's Principle always suffices and requires no guessing.

The usual approach — guess a particular solution shaped like b(t), trigonometric forcing gets a trigonometric guess — is inspired guessing. It works only for the small catalogue of b(t) whose derivatives close back on themselves (polynomials, exponentials, sines and cosines, products of those), and it silently fails otherwise. Duhamel is an algorithm: compute Φ, invert it, integrate.

What you give up is honest. §3.4.4 works the forced damped oscillator both ways and admits Duhamel doesn't necessarily come out better as a closed-form expression — the guessing method hands you the amplitude and phase directly. What Duhamel gives is a clear algorithmic way of calculating the answer, with the homogeneous problem solved first.

r.rot: your intro ODE class taught you to guess the answer's shape and solve for the coefficients. it works, when it works. the complaint here is that it's a bag of special cases dressed up as a method — and it dies the moment b(t) isn't on the list. duhamel is one formula that eats any continuous b. the tradeoff: you trade a clever shortcut for an integral you might not be able to evaluate in closed form.
r.ex: §3.4.4 does the damped forced oscillator by guessing y<sub>p</sub> = A cos(ω<sub>f</sub>t + φ) and burns a page on trig identities to extract A and φ. The text's own aside: memorizing trigonometric relations is not everyone's favorite pastime.
r.why: It's a stance about what counts as a method. A procedure that terminates on every input beats a heuristic with a lookup table, even when the heuristic is faster on the examples in the textbook — that's the same reason the book built the fundamental matrix in the first place.
r.math: Undetermined coefficients requires b in the span of a finite-dimensional space closed under d/dt. Duhamel requires only b continuous.

cards.q: Specialize Duhamel to an autonomous system. What does the resulting formula say about the role of each piece?
cards.a:
Remark 3.4.5. With Φ(t) = e(t−t₀)A, the product Φ(t)Φ(s)−1 collapses by Theorem 3.1.8(ii)–(iii) to e(t−s)A, and the ugly Φ(t)∫Φ(s)−1⋅ becomes a convolution:
x(t) = e(t−t₀)Ax₀ + ∫t₀t e(t−s)Ab(s) ds  (3.33)
Read it as physics. e(t−s)A is the propagator: it transports a state from time s to time t. The forcing b(s)ds is an impulse delivered at time s; the system then evolves it forward for the remaining t − s.

So the solution is the initial condition propagated forward, plus every infinitesimal kick propagated forward from when it landed. Only the elapsed time t − s appears, which is exactly the statement that an autonomous system doesn't care what o'clock it is.

r.rot: e<sup>(t−s)A</sup> is a time machine: hand it a state and a duration, it evolves the state. the formula then reads like a ledger — where you started, carried forward to now, plus every nudge the forcing gave you, each carried forward from the moment it happened. superposition doing all the work. and notice only t − s shows up, never t and s separately: autonomous means the rules don't change over time.
r.ex: Example 3.4.7 uses this directly, replacing Φ(t)Φ<sup>−1</sup>(s) by Φ(t − s) before integrating — which is what turns a messy product of matrix exponentials into scalar integrals of e<sup>3t−2s</sup> and e<sup>−t+2s</sup>.
r.why: It is the finite-dimensional template for Duhamel throughout PDE and control theory, where the same formula holds with e<sup>(t−s)A</sup> a semigroup. The convolution form is also what makes transfer functions and frequency response possible.
r.math: Φ(t)Φ(s)<sup>−1</sup> = e<sup>(t−t₀)A</sup>e<sup>−(s−t₀)A</sup> = e<sup>(t−s)A</sup>. Nonautonomous: no such collapse, keep Φ(t)Φ(s)<sup>−1</sup>.

cards.q: Force a damped oscillator periodically. What is the amplitude of the steady response, and what does it warn you about?
cards.a:
For y″ + (b/m)y′ + ω₀²y = (F₀/m)cos(ωft), the particular solution yp = A cos(ωft + φ) has
A = (F₀/m) / √[(ω₀² − ωf²)² + ωf²b²/m²]  (3.37)
tan φ = (−ωfb/m) / (ω₀² − ωf²)  (3.38)
The amplitude depends not just on the forcing strength F₀ but on the forcing frequency, the natural frequency, the damping and the mass.

Resonance. Drive at ωf = ω₀ and the first term under the root vanishes, leaving A = F₀/(ωfb). As damping b → 0 that diverges. Remark 3.4.8: the unforced dynamics converge to zero; forced, it oscillates; forcing near the natural frequency gives the highest amplitude, and something very unpleasant will happen if you force at it.

The full solution is yh + yp, and yh = Ce−bt/2mcos(ω₀t + φ₀) dies. Only the forced part survives — the system forgets its initial condition and remembers only the driving.

r.rot: push a swing at random times, nothing much. push it once per swing — at its own frequency — and the amplitude climbs and climbs. the only thing stopping it is friction, and (3.37) says the peak height is basically forcing over damping. remove the damping and the formula goes to infinity, which is the math's way of saying the bridge comes down. also: the transient decays, so after a while the system is doing what you're telling it to, not what it started doing.
r.ex: The decaying homogeneous part is the transient, the y<sub>p</sub> part is the steady state. That split — transient forgotten, steady state dictated by the forcing — is why you can speak of 'the' frequency response of a stable linear system at all.
r.why: This is the practical reason anyone studies inhomogeneous linear systems. Resonance is the design constraint in buildings, bridges, circuits and rotating machinery, and the formula tells you the two levers you have: move ω₀ away from the forcing, or add damping.
r.math: A is maximized near ω<sub>f</sub> ≈ ω₀, peak ≈ F₀/(ω₀b). At ω<sub>f</sub> = ω₀, tanφ → ∞, so φ = −π/2: the response lags the drive by a quarter period.
